lead: Two random variables are independent when the value of one carries no information about the other. The joint distribution then factorizes: the probability of every pair is the product of the two marginal probabilities. This lets you multiply probabilities of separate measurements, split expectations into products, and justify the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. It is used in quality control, A/B tests, reliability of components, and in the normal models behind portfolio and signal-noise calculations.
prereq: You need: 4.1, 4.2, and independent events from Unit 2.

blocks.text: For discrete X and Y with joint pmf p(x,y) and marginals p_X(x)=P(X=x), p_Y(y)=P(Y=y), independence means p(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y) for every pair (x,y). Equivalently, the conditional pmf p<sub>Y|X</sub>(y|x)=p(x,y)/p_X(x) equals p_Y(y) whenever p_X(x)>0: learning X=x does not change the distribution of Y.
For continuous variables replace pmf by pdf f. Independence means f(x,y)=f_X(x)f_Y(y) for all x,y. The conditional density f<sub>Y|X</sub>(y|x)=f(x,y)/f_X(x) then equals f_Y(y).

The support, the set where the density is positive, must be a rectangle: a product of an x-interval and a y-interval. For example, f(x,y)=2 on 0<x<1, 0<y<1 has rectangular support. A triangular support forces dependence: for g(x,y)=2 on 0<x<y<1, the formula is constant, but Y must exceed X, so knowing X=0.9 forces Y>0.9.
From a table, multiply each row total by each column total. Every cell probability must equal that product. With counts, compare a cell with row total × column total ÷ grand total.
p(x,y) = p_X(x) p_Y(y) for all x, y
blocks.where: p(x,y) is the joint pmf; p_X and p_Y are the marginal pmfs of X and Y.

sections.h3: Products of functions, many variables, and pairwise traps

blocks.text: Independence passes through functions: if X and Y are independent, then g(X) and h(Y) are independent for fixed functions g and h. Therefore E[g(X)h(Y)] = E[g(X)]E[h(Y)] whenever the expectations exist. Setting g(x)=x and h(y)=y gives E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]. The converse is false: E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] does not prove independence; see 4.4.

For n variables X1,...,Xn, mutual independence means the joint pmf or pdf equals the product of all n marginals: f(x1,...,xn)=f1(x1)...fn(xn). Every subcollection must also factorize. For events A1,...,An, independence means P(A1∩...∩An)=P(A1)...P(An) and the same for every subcollection.

Pairwise independence only checks each pair. Toss two fair coins. Let A be first coin heads, B be second coin heads, C be the coins differ. Each pair is independent, but P(A∩B∩C)=0 while P(A)P(B)P(C)=1/8. Pairwise independence is not mutual independence.

items: Write the joint pmf or pdf and both marginals.
Mark the support. If it is not a rectangle, stop: dependent.
Multiply the marginals at a general point and compare with the joint.
If equal everywhere on the rectangle, independent; one unequal point proves dependence.
For a table, use row total × column total ÷ grand total.

blocks.text: Random sampling models observations as independent copies of one variable. Then the joint density is a product, so likelihoods multiply; this is used in maximum likelihood in Unit 5.

Reliability uses the product rule. Let p1 and p2 be the survival probabilities of two independent units. If the system survives when at least one unit survives (parallel redundancy), the survival probability is 1−(1−p1)(1−p2). If both units must survive (series), it is p1p2.

The law of large numbers and central limit theorem (4.5, 4.6) assume independent observations. In the multivariate normal (4.7), zero covariance plus normality gives independence, but that shortcut does not hold for other distributions.

figure.caption: Compare the joint with the product of the marginals. Agreement on a rectangular support leads to independence; one mismatch or a bent support means dependence.

spec.aria: A decision flow: compare the joint density with the product of the two marginals; agreement on a rectangular support gives independence, otherwise dependence.

examples.question: The random variables X and Y have joint density f(x,y)=6e<sup>−2x−3y</sup> for x>0, y>0. (a) Find the marginals f_X and f_Y. (b) Show X and Y are independent. (c) Find P(X>1, Y>2). (d) A second pair has g(x,y)=2 on 0<x<y<1. Find its marginals and show the pair is dependent.
steps: The support is the first quadrant x>0, y>0, a rectangle.
Product f_X(x)f_Y(y)=2e<sup>−2x</sup> · 3e<sup>−3y</sup> = 6e<sup>−2x−3y</sup> = f(x,y) for all x>0, y>0. Support is a rectangle, so X and Y are independent.

P(X>1, Y>2)=∫<sub>1</sub><sup>∞</sup>∫<sub>2</sub><sup>∞</sup> f dxdy = [∫<sub>1</sub><sup>∞</sup>2e<sup>−2x</sup> dx][∫<sub>2</sub><sup>∞</sup>3e<sup>−3y</sup> dy] = e<sup>−2</sup> · e<sup>−6</sup> = e<sup>−8</sup> ≈ 0.000335.
Product f_X(x)f_Y(y)=4y(1−x). At (x,y)=(0.25,0.5), joint=2 and product=4·0.5·0.75=1.5. Since 1.5≠2, dependent.
examples.answer: X and Y are independent with P(X>1,Y>2)=e<sup>−8</sup>≈0.000335; the second pair is dependent because its triangular support and product 4y(1−x) do not match g=2.
examples.check:
import math
p = round(math.exp(-8), 6)
print(p)
print(2.0)
print(1.5)

traps: Checking only the formula: 6e<sup>−2x−3y</sup> splits, but a density on a triangle can also split. Check the support shape.
Forgetting 'for all x,y': equality at one point proves nothing; one unequal point proves dependence.
Using counts instead of probabilities in a table: compare a cell count with row total × column total ÷ grand total.
Confusing pairwise with mutual independence. For three or more variables, every subcollection must factorize.
Assuming E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] proves independence. It only proves zero covariance; dependence can hide in higher moments.

quiz.q: State the discrete condition for X and Y to be independent.
Why does a triangular support force dependence?
quiz.a: The possible values of one variable depend on the other, so the support is not a product set and the conditional distribution changes with the condition.

quiz.q: X and Y take values 0 or 1 with joint probabilities p(0,0)=0.12, p(0,1)=0.18, p(1,0)=0.28, p(1,1)=0.42. Are X and Y independent?
quiz.a: Marginals: P(X=0)=0.30, P(X=1)=0.70; P(Y=0)=0.40, P(Y=1)=0.60. Products: 0.12, 0.18, 0.28, 0.42. They match every cell, so independent.

quiz.q: For the independent pair in the worked example, find P(X>0.5, Y>1).
Let f(x,y)=c(x+y) on 0<x<1, 0<y<1. Find c and decide whether X and Y are independent.
quiz.a: Integrate: c∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup>∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup>(x+y)dxdy=c, so c=1. Marginals are f_X(x)=x+1/2 and f_Y(y)=y+1/2. Product is not x+y, so dependent.

quiz.q: Give three events that are pairwise independent but not mutually independent.
quiz.a: Toss two fair coins: A=first heads, B=second heads, C=coins differ. Every pair has probability 1/4=1/2·1/2, but A∩B∩C is impossible, so joint probability 0≠1/8.

quiz.q: If X and Y are independent, why is E[XY]=E[X]E[Y]?
quiz.a: Take g(x)=x and h(y)=y in E[g(X)h(Y)]=E[g(X)]E[h(Y)].

beyond: Not for the exam. Independence is a modelling assumption, not a fact you can read from data without testing. Practitioners use mutual information, chi-square tests of independence, and residual checks to detect dependence. In machine learning, naive Bayes assumes independent features given the class, and the assumption often works despite being false. In finance, independence across assets fails in crashes, so copulas are used to model dependence. Search next for mutual information, copulas, and conditional independence.
